PAPER: Journal of Academic Ethics (2026) 24:14 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09691-3 Beyond Detection: How Students Use—and Hide—AI in Online Assessments and What Authentic Tasks Can Do About It Oleg Kirsanov1 · Lovleen Kushwah1 · Geethanjali Selvaretnam1 Received: 3 July 2025 / Accepted: 8 October 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract As AI tools such as ChatGPT and CoPilot become increasingly common in higher edu- cation, universities must reconsider how assessments are designed, monitored, and sup- ported. This small case study investigates how students use AI in online assessments, whether they disclose such use, and how ethical concerns shape their behaviour. Based on a targeted survey of undergraduate economics students, representing about 18% of the cohort (31/174), we find that only about one-third reported using AI tools, this figure is lower than those reported in several larger surveys. Most reported uses were supportive tasks such as rewording or idea generation. Some students appear to opt out early, suggest- ing a strategic decision to avoid scrutiny. Fear of penalties is widespread, and exploratory modelling suggests that students with greater ethical concerns may be less likely to use AI at all. At the same time, students express support for guidance and structured regulation. Many favour citation rules and believe AI can be used ethically. Real-world, data-based tasks are widely seen as a way to reduce misuse of AI. The way to tackle the negative learning effects of AI is not by eliminating AI, but by encouraging meaningful engage- ment. We conclude that students are navigating institutional ambiguity with caution and pragmatism. Overall, our conclusions are preliminary and exploratory: findings are not generalisable, but they point to promising directions for assessment design. Rather than relying on detection and deterrence, universities may achieve better outcomes by aligning assessments with authentic tasks and clear expectations—and by addressing fairness about all students’ access and use of AI. Kirsanov et al. Introduction The rise of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Microsoft CoPilot, and Google Gemini has triggered widespread concern and confusion across higher education. While educators debate how to preserve academic integrity (White, 2023), students are already adapting: using AI for brainstorming, rewriting, coding support, and, in some cases, generating full responses in online assessments (Stone, 2024; Sublime & Renna, 2024). Recent evidence from Hungary shows Gen-Z undergraduates express strong ethical ambivalence toward ChatGPT despite widespread familiarity (Fajt & Schiller, 2025). But how do students them- selves understand the ethics of these tools? When do they disclose their use, and when do they remain silent? And what kinds of assessments might encourage honest, productive engagement with AI rather than concealment or evasion? Recent studies have begun mapping this terrain at scale (e.g. Gustilo et al., 2024; John- ston et al., 2024; Leaton Gray et al., 2025), yet they typically rely on single-pass question- naires that cannot reveal how students strategically avoid disclosure of AI use or how they view specific assessment formats. Our study addresses precisely those blind spots. This paper investigates how students perceive and use AI tools in the context of university assessments. Drawing on a targeted survey administered to economics undergraduates, we examine not only whether students use AI, but how they describe its purpose, whether they disclose it, and what ethical or institutional concerns shape their choices. We also explore how students think AI should be regulated—and whether alternative assessment formats might reduce misuse by design rather than deterrence. Our work complements recent stud- ies on disclosure, motivation, and institutional ambiguity in the wake of generative AI adop- tion in higher education (e.g. Fawns et al., 2024; Fleckenstein et al., 2024; Freeman, 2025; Stone, 2024), but also adds a behavioural dimension by tracking early opt-out patterns and collecting student reflections on specific assessment formats. Our contribution is modest but of value. Rather than estimating sector-wide prevalence, we use a small, discipline-specific case study to illuminate behavioural dynamics around AI use. A feature that large one-shot surveys struggle to observe, which our study is able to show is an early “opt-out” (funnel) pattern, where many respondents declare non-use at the first opportunity and therefore never face follow-ups about purpose or disclosure. We inter- pret this as strategic non-disclosure consistent with policy ambiguity and penalty anxiety (e.g., Fawns et al., 2024; Stone, 2024), and we connect it to students’ views on assessment formats. The aim is not generalisation, but to inform practical course-level design choices. While national surveys such as Freeman (2025) capture the scale and diversity of student AI use, our study moves from breadth to depth in three ways. First, by focusing on a single disciplinary cohort—final-year economics students—we trace a behavioural funnel: many respondents declare non-use of AI at the first available opportunity, a pattern invisible in large cross-sectional datasets. This pattern aligns with recent findings that students often “strategically opt out” of disclosure under unclear institutional norms (Gonsalves, 2025; Stone, 2024). Second, we link AI use to ethical concerns, showing that disclosure is shaped more by uncertainty and fear of penalties than by beliefs about right or wrong. Third, we examine how students reflect on different types of assessment, and how these formats such as data-based tasks may reduce misuse by making AI shortcuts less effective. These insights 1 3 Beyond Detection: How Students Use—and Hide—AI in Online… Page 3 of 23 14 point toward concrete design strategies that align assessment with thoughtful engagement— an area often overlooked in policy debates (Gonsalves, 2025; Watkins, 2024). We find that AI use is non-trivial—about one-third of respondents admit some use—yet disclosure is rare. Many students opted out of reporting AI use early in the survey, and even among those who admitted use, only a few said they would always disclose it. This silence does not appear to reflect dishonesty; rather, it reflects rational caution in the face of ambiguous policies and perceived academic risk. These results echo broader evidence that non-disclosure is often a rational response to unclear expectations, not a simple violation of integrity norms (Fawns et al., 2024; Freeman, 2025; Stone, 2024). At the same time, students are not calling for a free pass. Most respondents agreed that AI can be acceptable when used supportively, and many welcomed clearer citation rules and institutional guidance, which is in alignment with existing literature (Freeman, 2025). Ethi- cal concerns—about fairness, learning, or detection—were present but unevenly distrib- uted. What stood out was students’ fear of being penalised for AI use, even when the use was moderate or constructive. This “penalty anxiety” is also consistently reported in recent UK and international surveys (Freeman, 2025; Oc et al., 2024; Stone, 2024). Large UK surveys report parallel demand for university-wide policies (Johnston et al., 2024). The most promising results came from student responses to assessment design. Many supported the idea that meaningful, data-rich tasks reduce overreliance on AI—not by ban- ning it, but by setting questions. As AI tools become increasingly accessible, universities face urgent questions–not just about detection and enforcement, but about transparency, pedagogy, and trust. This study highlights three key findings. First, while reported AI use was moderate, disclosure was rare, driven more by fear of penalties than intent to deceive. Second, students used AI mainly for supportive tasks like rewording or idea generation, and many called for clearer citation rules to distinguish acceptable from unacceptable use. Third, students valued assessments that emphasised real-world data and interpretation–tasks where shallow AI shortcuts fall short. basic or careless use of AI offers little real benefit. This aligns with current proposals for “authentic” assessment design in the AI era (Gon- salves, 2025; Watkins, 2024). Interestingly, some students who disagreed with this premise offered even stronger arguments in favour of real-world tasks—not because they deter AI, but because they provide a context where AI becomes a learning aid, not a shortcut. This paper contributes to ongoing debates in education policy, academic integrity, and student behaviour. It shows that students are strategic, attentive to institutional cues, and often eager for clear, constructive guidance. We add empirical depth to the emerging con- versation on generative-AI ethics by documenting early opt-out behaviour, developing a composite index of students’ ethical anxiety and foregrounding student support for authen- tic assessments. Our results suggest that the most effective way to manage AI in education may not be through detection and punishment, but through smarter assessment design and transparent norms. Section 3 presents the analysis and results on AI use, disclosure behaviour, and student beliefs about assessment design. Methods Survey Design and Data Collection We administered a short online survey in Spring 2025 to final-year undergraduate econom- ics students at the University of Glasgow. This targeted survey focused on students’ experi- ences with online assessments, use of AI tools, and related ethical concerns. This research has been approved by the College of Social Sciences Research Ethics Committee at the University of Glasgow. The questionnaire combined multiple-choice and Likert-scale items, with optional com- ment boxes for qualitative insights. Students were first asked whether they had completed any online assessments, and only those who answered “yes” continued to the main section on AI use. Subsequent questions asked whether students had used AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT or CoPilot) in online assessments, what purposes they used them for (e.g., brainstorming, rewording, coding, or full-answer generation), and whether they would disclose such use to instructors. Additional items measured ethical concerns (e.g., fairness, learning impact, penalties) and policy beliefs (e.g., whether AI should be banned or allowed with guidance). One final question asked students whether real-world, data-based tasks might reduce over- reliance on AI tools. Appendix A provides a structured list of all survey questions used in the analysis, along with response distributions. Each question is assigned a short reference label (e.g., , plans , ), which is used in bold throughout the text to refer to specific AI use disclosure survey items. Participants were recruited through course announcements and email invitations, and participation was voluntary and anonymous. Of the 174 students approached, a total of 31 responded to the survey (18%). This small response rate implies potential self-selection bias. Participation itself may be impacted by students’ attitudes to online assessment or AI. Furthermore several AI-specific items were only asked of self-declared users, further amplifying selection into sub-modules of the questionnaire. We therefore treat all estimates as exploratory and descriptive. In terms of demographics, 55% of respondents identified as female (compared with about 40% in the full cohort) and 45% as international students (compared with about 25% in the full cohort). This suggests that international students, and to a lesser extent female students, were somewhat over-represented among respondents. Given the small sample size, we treat these figures as descriptive only, but they indicate potential self-selection bias in survey participation. The questionnaire used branching logic. All respondents answered core items on online assessment experiences; only those indicating that they had completed online assessments saw the AI section; and only self-declared AI users saw follow-ups on purposes and disclo- sure. Consequently, non-reach of some questions reflects the designed funnel rather than missing data. Statistical Analysis Survey data were organised and coded in MATLAB. All Likert responses were converted to numeric values (1–5) where 1 is strongly Disagree and 5 is strongly agree. We com- 1 3 Beyond Detection: How Students Use—and Hide—AI in Online… Page 5 of 23 14 puted descriptive statistics (frequencies, means, cross-tabs) for each question to character- ize students’ AI use, disclosure, and beliefs. Unless stated otherwise, percentages reported for Likert items refer to the share of respondents selecting each category among those who reached that item. To further analyse the students’ concerns about AI use, we constructed a multi-item atti- tude scales following established practice for creating latent measures from attitudinal items by following (Warmbrod, 2014). This composite index which we refer to as Ethical Anxiety Index, is based on four Likert items measuring ethical concerns (about unfair access to AI, ease of detection, penalty anxiety, and whether AI undermines learning). This is explained in detail in Section 3.4. For inferential analysis, we explored predictors of AI use through a logistic regression model. The regression model used listwise deletion of cases with missing data. Model coef- ficients, odds ratios, and confidence intervals are reported in the Results section. Given the small sample size, these analyses are treated as exploratory, with findings interpreted cau- tiously, according to Hosmer et al. (2013). Qualititative Data Integration The questionnaire’s optional comment boxes allowed students to explain or elaborate on their answers in free text. These open-ended responses were reviewed manually: responses were scanned for recurrent themes or illustrative viewpoints, which were used to contextu- alize the quantitative findings. Key ideas from the comments were noted alongside the sur- vey results (e.g. students’ own rationales for preferring authentic tasks). We did not attempt formal coding of these short responses given the small number of comments; rather, qualita- tive input was used illustratively to enrich interpretation of the survey data. Results Student Use of AI Of the 31 students who responded to our survey, 2 indicated that they had not completed any online assessments (Q3: Online Assessment) and were therefore excluded from further questions on AI use. This left a sample of 29 students. When asked whether they had ever used AI tools (such as ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot) to assist with online assessments (Q4: AI Use), 18 students explicitly answered “No”, while 1 student left the question blank—which we interpret as effectively equivalent to a “No.” This means that only 10 students (approximately 34%) acknowledged having used AI tools, and only these students were presented with follow-up questions on purpose and disclosure. Notably, among the 13 international students, 10 reported not using AI, 2 left the ques- tion blank, and only 1 student reported using AI. Among the 17 UK nationals, by contrast, 8 reported using AI—a substantially higher proportion—while 1 student left the question blank and 8 reported not using AI. This branching structure creates an immediate funnel: most students either stated they had not used AI or avoided the question altogether at the first opportunity. While this might superficially be read as low incidence of AI use, we argue that it more likely reflects strate- 1 3 14 Page 6 of 23 O. Kirsanov et al. gic non-engagement. Given current uncertainty about institutional policy, potential penal- ties, and reputational risks, it is arguably rational for students to “exit early” by declaring non-use—especially when disclosure might be interpreted as an admission of wrongdo- ing. This behaviour aligns with recent findings that students often engage in strategic self- presentation when institutional expectations are ambiguous as well as in self-preservation (Fawns et al., 2024; Stone, 2024). Our estimated AI-use share ( 34% among those who reached Q4) is lower than rates ∼ typically reported in larger, cross-disciplinary surveys (often 60–70%). Two, non-exclu- ∼ sive explanations are plausible here: (i) discipline/context effects–final-year economics coursework in our programme emphasises structured reasoning and data analysis, which may invite supportive rather than generative use; and (ii) underreporting–consistent with our observed early opt-out, students with higher ethical anxiety or perceived penalty risk may rationally choose non-disclosure. We flag this as a limitation and caution against gen- eralising prevalence from this small, single-programme sample. For the subset who did report using AI tools, we asked what purposes they used them for (Q5: Purpose of Use). We gave a list to choose all that applied and anything else. Their responses are shown in Fig. 1. The most common use was to proofread for spelling/grammar and for better wording and structure. A small percentage had used AI to help with searching for literature. Another use that students pointed to was to brainstorm ideas. Importantly, no students reported using AI to generate an entire answer and submit it as their own—the most ethically contentious form of use. These patterns suggest that declared AI use is relatively low in incidence and largely support-focused in nature. Students who disclosed usage appear to treat AI tools more like spell-checkers, search engines, or brainstorming partners than substitutes for their own work. Open-text comments about why they used AI in the way they did (Q6: AI Use Views) reinforce this view. Several students described using AI to improve clarity, manage time pressure, or compensate for difficulties in written expression. Given that almost everyone around me uses it to get a competitive edge, I’d be foolish not to use it myself.” Such comments reveal a complex landscape of motivations—from learning support and accessibility to competitive pressure. They also underscore the tension between institutional silence on AI use and students’ pragmatic attempts to balance performance, fairness, and risk. The rarity of students reaching this stage in the survey, however, raises important ques- tions about who chose to declare use and under what perceived conditions. These issues are explored further in the following sections on disclosure behaviour and ethical concerns. Disclosure Behaviour: The Missing Middle Students who reported using AI tools were asked whether they would disclose this use to instructors (Q7: Disclosure Behaviour). As shown in Fig. 2, responses cluster around “sometimes" and “always," but the most striking feature is the large group who never reached this question—not due to missing data, but because they had previously declared non-use (in other words, those who exited early). While the majority of respondents did not reach this disclosure question, this absence is not simply missing data—it is behaviourally meaningful. Students had already distanced themselves from AI use earlier in the survey (Q6: AI Use), and we cannot distinguish between true non-users and those who strategically avoid disclosure. For those who did admit to AI use, disclosure appears to be hesitant but not absent: most were willing to dis- close at least sometimes, though only a small minority claimed they would always do so. This pattern reflects a broader point: in the current climate of ambiguous university guid- ance, unclear enforcement, and potential reputational or academic risk, it is rational for stu- dents to avoid disclosure altogether. Even among those who see AI as useful or legitimate, openly declaring its use may not be in their best interest. As noted earlier, this mirrors a classic coordination problem: in the absence of clear institutional norms or incentives, the dominant strategy may simply be silence. In game-theoretic terms, disclosure collapses to a Nash equilibrium of non-disclosure—not because students are necessarily dishonest, but because the payoff structure rewards non-disclosure. 1 3 14 Page 8 of 23 O. These results support the interpretation that non-disclosure is not random or evasive, but a rational response to institutional ambiguity and perceived risk— reinforcing our earlier point that silence is an equilibrium strategy in the current environment. Looking ahead, this has clear policy implications. If most students remain silent even when they believe their AI use is legitimate, then disclosure will continue to be rare—and institutions will struggle to distinguish between supportive, misleading, and non-existent use. Without a shift in norms, disclosure may remain a dominated strategy. What is needed is a clearer policy framework, including transparent guidance on citation, boundaries for acceptable use, and a shift toward normalising responsible AI support in coursework. With- out these changes, students may continue to behave rationally—but in ways that undermine trust, clarity, and learning. The strategic silence we observe raises an obvious question: What rules or norms would students actually support if institutions clarified them? The next subsection therefore turns to students’ stated views on the acceptability of AI under different policy scenarios. Acceptability of AI use To understand how students view the evolving role of AI tools in academic work, we asked them to respond to three broad policy statements in Q8: AI Acceptable: (1) AI is accept- able if used for support but not to generate full answers, (2) AI should not be allowed at all in graded assessments, and (3) AI use should be encouraged provided citation guidance is given. These questions were answered by 29 students. Students rated their agreement with each of these statements on a five-point Likert scale. As Fig. 3 shows, there is broad support for moderate, well-regulated AI use. These results support the interpretation that students are not simply trying to “get away with” AI use. Instead, they express a nuanced understanding of appropriate boundaries. They accept AI as a tool, but want clarity on when and how it may be used—especially in assessed contexts. The desire for citation guidance signals that students are not opposed to transparency, but may lack the framework or confidence to disclose use voluntarily, as seen in earlier sections. Does Ethical Anxiety Predict AI Disclosure? The central behavioural pattern we explore in this study is selective disclosure of AI use. In Section 3.1, we found that many students choose an early “No" when asked whether they had ever used AI tools, a behaviour we interpret as strategic self-presentation or deliber- ate non-disclosure rather than definitive proof of non-use. Given the ambiguity in institu- tional policy and the potential reputational or academic risks involved, students’ decisions to report or conceal AI usage are likely influenced by their own ethical concerns and perceived anxieties about fairness, penalties, or learning integrity. To quantitatively examine the factors that predict this disclosure decision, we first con- structed a binary dependent variable from survey question Q4: AI Use (“Have you ever used AI tools to assist with online assessments?”). Students who answered either “Yes, and I believe my usage followed the guidelines," or “Yes, but I am not sure whether my usage was allowed" were coded as having disclosed AI use (coded as 1). Students who explicitly answered “No” or provided no response at all were coded as not having disclosed AI use (coded as 0). Thus, our dependent variable ( ) captures students’ self-reported dis- AIuser closure of AI usage rather than factual or actual usage. This aligns with our funnel analysis, which showed a significant number of students strategically choosing non-disclosure at the earliest opportunity. Our primary predictor variable captures students’ ethical anxieties about AI use. Measur- ing ethical anxiety in a consistent and reliable way is inherently challenging, as anxiety can encompass different aspects of ethical and practical concern. To address this complexity, we used four Likert-scale items from question Q9: Ethical Concerns, each asking students to rate their agreement with statements about specific anxieties related to AI: fear of penalties, unfair access, undermining learning, and ease of detection. Each item represents a distinct but potentially overlapping dimension of ethical anxiety. This set of questions was answered by 29 students. A complementary construct, AI guilt, was recently used by Qu and Wang (2025) as the average of three items (rationalisation tendencies, perceived social norms, and perceived 1 3 Beyond Detection: How Students Use—and Hide—AI in Online… Page 11 of 23 14 AI access is unfair Worried about penalties AI undermines learning Easy to detect AI work 0 5 10 15 20 25 30 Percentage of respondents Disagree Neutral Agree Fig. 4 Student concerns around fairness, learning, penalties, and detection risk of detection).1 We keep the term “ethical anxiety” to signal this conceptual difference, but in the robustness section we report that replacing our index with their item-set (re-scaled to our sample) leaves the main results unchanged. Figure 4 shows the distribution of responses to these four anxiety items. Anxiety about penalties was the most widespread concern, with about three-quarters of respondents agree- ing or strongly agreeing they would worry about being penalized if they used AI. Anxiety about unfair access to better AI tools was also common, with around half of respondents expressing concern. Views about AI undermining learning were mixed, reflecting diverse student perspectives, while concerns about ease of detection were least prevalent. This range of responses mirrors recent international findings, which show similar patterns of mixed anxiety across penalty, fairness, and learning dimensions (Fajt & Schiller, 2025). Given this complexity, constructing a single ethical anxiety measure from these four survey items is not straightforward. If the four questions reliably measured the same under- lying anxiety dimension, creating a single index would be simple: we could just average stu- dents’ answers. But we first needed to check whether these four questions indeed measure essentially the same thing or whether they tap into several distinct concerns. To examine this, we employed two common statistical tests: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Cronbach’s alpha. First, we ran a Principal Component Analysis (PCA), a standard statistical approach to identify whether multiple survey items can be meaningfully reduced into fewer latent (underlying) dimensions.2 We found that the first latent dimension identified by the PCA explained approximately 46% of the total variability in the four anxiety questions. However, the contributions of the individual questions to this dimension were uneven. Second, we computed Cronbach’s alpha, a widely-used statistic that checks whether multiple survey questions reliably measure the same concept (Cronbach, 1951). A value of alpha close to 1 indicates good reliability (the items are consistent and interchangeable), whereas values close to zero or negative indicate poor reliability (the items measure fun- damentally different things). In our case, alpha was strongly negative (α= 4.15), clearly − indicating that simply averaging these four items into one index would not be appropriate. This contrasts with Qu and Wang (2025), whose three guilt items formed a highly coherent scale (α=0.71) in a much larger Singaporean sample (n = 193). The divergence reinforces our decision to retain a dual measure rather than force uni-dimensionality. Taken together, these results suggest that students’ anxieties about ethical use of AI are multidimensional: students simultaneously experience concerns about fairness, learning integrity, and penalties, but these concerns are distinct enough to make a simple average misleading. Therefore we decided to adopt a dual approach to capture ethical anxiety: first, we con- structed a simple and intuitive “Ethical Anxiety Index: Average" calculated as the nor- malised mean of the four Likert-scale items (scaled between 0 and 1, following Warmbrod, 2014); second, we used the empirically derived first principal component as a latent, explor- atory measure of ethical anxiety, “Ethical Anxiety Index: PC1". This dual approach allowed us to examine disclosure behaviour through two lenses: a straightforward average captur- ing broad anxiety, and an empirically weighted PCA score highlighting dominant anxiety dimensions. We then conducted exploratory logistic regressions using each of these anxiety measures to predict whether students disclosed their AI use. Given our small sample size (only 27 stu- dents have answered anxiety measures related questions and participated in online assess- ments), we considered a limited number of additional control variables, including gender, native-English status, and home status (UK-based vs. international). We retained only those variables that substantially improved model fit and offered clear theoretical insights. The home status variable (UK vs non-UK) notably improved explanatory power and was statistically significant, indicating that UK nationals disclosed AI use significantly more fre- quently. Conversely, gender, and native English status4 showed no statistically significant or substantively meaningful effects and were therefore excluded from the final analysis. Hence, our final regression models include only ethical anxiety and home status as predictors. Overall, these exploratory results reinforce our broader interpretation: ethical anxiety– particularly around fairness, penalties, and learning–may encourage students to strategi- cally avoid disclosing AI use, although our modest sample size limits statistical precision. Additionally, the substantial impact of home status suggests notable cultural or institutional differences in how students navigate ambiguity around AI use. These findings align closely with the strategic disclosure patterns discussed earlier and underscore the importance of clear institutional policies to address uncertainty. Taken together, strategic non-disclosure and anxieties about policy leave universities with a dilemma: detection alone will not build trust, yet blanket bans are unpopular. A con- structive path may lie in redesigning assessments so that transparent, responsible AI use is rewarded. We therefore asked students whether “real-world, data-rich tasks” could reduce over-reliance on AI and analysed their qualitative responses, which is presented next. Real-World Assessments as a Way Forward We asked students to evaluate the following statement: “In online exams, using real-world data makes the task more meaningful and reduces the likelihood of over-relying on AI tools” through Likert question Q10: Assessment Design, and the follow-up open-text question Q11: Assessment Design Belief. Responses to Q10 revealed considerable optimism: of the 31 respondents, 58 % agreed or strongly agreed, and only 10 % explicitly disagreed. Such widespread agreement sug- gests students see authentic, data-rich assessments as a promising approach to reducing superficial or unreflective AI use. 1 3 14 Page 14 of 23 O. Kirsanov et al. Four Shades of Student Opinion Student comments elaborating on this belief revealed a nuanced landscape of perspectives, summarised in Table 2. Approximately one-third of respondents viewed authentic datasets primarily as a deterrent to AI misuse, while another subset believed that these assessments encourage constructive and responsible use of AI. Others argued that effectiveness depends significantly on disciplinary context, with some suggesting that intrinsic ethical standards ultimately outweigh assessment formats in shaping academic integrity. Why Data Help–And Why They Sometimes Don’t Among those who supported the use of real-world data tasks, the dominant rationale centred on friction and fairness. These students argued that current large language models (LLMs) remain limited in handling complex numerical problems or nuanced datasets. By increasing the effort and complexity of leveraging AI to shortcut assessments, authentic data effec- tively “level the playing field.” As one respondent noted: "AI systems don’t seem to be very good at understanding material or providing accu- rate answers (even to simple numerical problems). Thus, as long as AI isn’t very competent, the playing field seems to be level when undertaking data-based tasks." It is precisely the kind of sentiment we had in mind when designing this question: that making assessments more meaningful and open-ended might naturally reduce the tempta- tion to outsource them to AI. However, comments from students who disagreed revealed something we may have underestimated: that data-rich tasks do not necessarily reduce AI use—they may instead amplify its value, especially for students working under time con- straints. As instructors, we introduced this idea because we believed real-world data would promote authentic, original work. For educators, this is not a failure—it is a rec- ognition that students are entering a world where AI is embedded in professional problem- solving. The implication is not to eliminate AI use, but to ensure that assessments reward skillful, responsible application of such tools.5 Finally, some students pointed to intrinsic ethical standards as the determining factor for responsible AI use, rather than the assessment format itself. These respondents argued that students predisposed to unethical practices would persist irrespective of the assessment design: “I don’t think so... AI weaknesses, Academic Integrity, and Design Principles While students expressed different views about whether data-based assessments reduce reli- ance on AI tools, two consistent issues came through in many responses. First, several students highlighted that current AI tools often perform poorly on tasks involving real data. The AI tools struggle with numerical accuracy, complex data format- ting, and applied interpretation. This perceived weakness is one reason why some students believe that data-rich tasks discourage blind reliance on AI. Second, students raised concerns about academic integrity – specifically, whether AI- generated responses are being passed off as original work by some students. In response, students proposed several concrete design principles aimed at ensuring that assessments reflect genuine student effort. They recommended that datasets be modified or synthesised to prevent standard AI systems from generating generic solutions. Requiring code submis- sion or brief explanatory videos could help instructors verify that students had engaged deeply with the material and understood their own process. Context-specific or current- event prompts were also suggested as a means of making AI-generated answers less appli- cable. Structuring group assignments with defined roles and accountability mechanisms was likewise advised to support transparent and equitable collaboration. Importantly, these recommendations do not suggest that AI should be banned from assessments. Rather, they reflect a student view that assessments should reward thoughtful, transparent use of AI, while discouraging superficial or uncritical reliance. Recent empirical studies support this approach, demonstrating that AI-generated essays can achieve grades comparable to those of human-written work and can evade current detection methods (Rev- ell et al., 2024). This reinforces the argument that smart, proactive assessment design is preferable to reactive policing. In sum, authentic, data-intensive assessments–when intentionally structured to promote interpretation, critical reasoning, and personal engagement–can diminish the value of superfi- cial AI shortcuts and encourage more responsible and skilful use of AI tools. Such assessments cannot entirely eliminate concerns about fairness or integrity, but they offer a promising avenue for fostering constructive engagement with AI in the evolving landscape of higher education. These findings, when viewed alongside the broader patterns of disclosure behaviour and ethical concerns explored earlier, point to important tensions and opportunities in how insti- tutions might foster transparency, trust in student work, and constructive AI use through both policy and assessment design, a theme we now examine in the Discussion. Discussion This study sets out to understand how students use AI tools in online assessments, what ethi- cal boundaries they perceive, and how they navigate institutional uncertainty. Our results paint a picture of cautious engagement: while about one-third of students report using AI tools for supportive purposes like idea generation or rewording, none reported using AI to generate full answers, and only a few said they would always disclose their use. This mir- rors national trends: surveys consistently show high rates of light-touch AI use, especially for drafting or checking work, but much lower levels of disclosure (Freeman, 2025; Stone, 2024). 1 3 Beyond Detection: How Students Use—and Hide—AI in Online… Page 17 of 23 14 It is important to emphasise that these results are exploratory and drawn from a small case study. With only 31 respondents from a single disciplinary programme, the findings are not generalisable, but they can illuminate patterns that may warrant closer examination in larger, multi-institutional samples. One of the most striking findings is how many students chose to “opt out” early in the survey by indicating they had not used AI at all. While some of these students may be genu- ine non-users, the survey structure allowed us to observe a behavioural pattern: students were given an early opportunity to disassociate from AI, and many took them. From an economic perspective, this behaviour is consistent with a rational strategy under uncertainty. With ambiguous university policies, unclear enforcement, and reputational risk, disclosure may not be in a student’s best interest—even when their use of AI is pedagogically harm- less. This is supported by recent qualitative studies in both the UK and Australia, which find that students often operate under perceived risk, and develop personal “rules” to avoid detection or accusation (Fawns et al., 2024; Stone, 2024). The proportion of students in our survey who reported using AI tools (about one-third) is lower than the levels typically observed in larger, cross-disciplinary studies, which often find a majority of students experimenting with generative AI. Two factors may explain this discrepancy. First, disciplinary context: economics assessments in this programme empha- sise structured reasoning and data analysis, which may favour supportive over generative uses. Second, underreporting: consistent with our observed “early opt-out” funnel, students with higher ethical anxiety may have chosen not to disclose use of AI at all. Among students who did admit to AI use, most said they would disclose “sometimes,” a few “always,” and one “never.” But the vast majority of respondents never reached that question at all—again, not because they refused to answer, but because they had already denied using AI. This pattern suggests behaviour is shaped not only by personal beliefs but by institutional signalling: in the absence of clear expectations, non-disclosure becomes the safest response. Recent governance research by Coates et al. (2025) shows that universities lacking clear, board-level academic-integrity indicators face precisely this incentive vacuum, thereby foster- ing student “strategic compliance.” Their multi-institutional framework reinforces our finding that disclosure decisions reflect perceived governance strength rather than individual morals alone. In turn, these governance-level insights are consistent with the literature on “strategic compliance” in academic integrity, where students respond not to absolute rules, but to their interpretation of institutional cues (Freeman, 2025; Gonsalves, 2025). Qualitative work in Australia likewise shows students normalise peer “help” while othering perceived cheaters, reinforcing our finding that norms, not rules, drive behaviour (Leaton Gray et al., 2025). At the same time, students do not appear hostile to AI itself. Responses to the Q8: AI Acceptable question reveal broad support for the idea that AI can be used appropriately in academic work—especially when used as a support tool, or when guided by clear citation rules. There is far less agreement with the idea that AI should be banned altogether in graded assessments. This reflects recent national and international findings: students want clarity, not freedom from rules. Many actively support the development of citation norms and AI literacy training (Freeman, 2025; Oc et al., 2024). When we asked students to rate specific ethical concerns—such as whether AI under- mines learning, creates unfair access, or is hard to detect—we found a mix of opinions. Penalty anxiety was the most widespread concern, followed by fairness. These findings are echoed across the sector: fear of misconduct accusations is the single strongest deter- 1 3 14 Page 18 of 23 O. Kirsanov et al. rent to AI use reported by students in recent surveys (Freeman, 2025; Stone, 2024). Our exploratory regression analyses supported this qualitatively, showing a consistent negative relationship—albeit statistically marginal, given the small sample—between ethical anxiety and the likelihood of disclosure. Critically, home status emerged as a significant predictor of disclosure, with UK-based students significantly more willing to disclose AI use than their international counterparts. This points to important cultural or institutional differences that universities must explicitly consider when developing policies and communication strate- gies around AI. One plausible interpretation is that international students perceive the stakes of academic integrity breaches as especially high, which heightens their ethical anxiety and makes disclosure less attractive. Prior research has noted similar dynamics, though differ- ences in students’ previous academic experiences and understandings of institutional norms may also contribute (Sanni-Anibire et al., 2021). International students may not be confident of the AI norms of the university and decide to either opt out or not reveal. These disclosure patterns also need to be understood in light of the institutional policy context. At the time of data collection, the University of Glasgow had a dedicated web page which articulated broad principles on generative AI use, captured by the statement, “we want to support you in learning how to use these tools effectively, ethically, critically, and transparently.” The guidelines are deliberately not regimented at the central level, allowing course leaders in charge of assessments to decide the extent to which AI may or may not be used, according to what they think is best for the students. On the other hand, students were cautioned that “AI tools … are prone to biases, inaccuracies and mistakes.” Such broad but cautionary principles can plausibly heightened students’ uncertainty and help explain why even supportive uses were rarely disclosed. Not having specific rules can leave room for students to be confused about differences in AI guidance across assessments. Some course leaders may make the guidance very clear for each assessment while others may be too vague or just point students to the central web page. Finally, one of the most promising insights came from student reactions to the idea of using real-world data in assessments. While most respondents agreed that this could reduce overreliance on AI, the accompanying comments revealed something deeper: data-rich, meaningful tasks don’t simply deter AI use—they reframe it. Students who disagreed with the statement often did so not because they rejected the value of such assessments, but because they saw them as places where AI can legitimately enhance work. This reflects a shift seen in current educational literature: authentic tasks are not cheat-proof, but they shift the challenge from concealment to competence (Gonsalves, 2025; Watkins, 2024). This observation points to a constructive way forward. If institutions want to manage the risks of AI without banning it outright, the design of assessments must evolve. Gov- ernance scholars likewise argue that authentic, integrity-centred assessment design must be embedded in institution-wide reform agendas rather than left to isolated course teams (Coates et al., 2025). Tasks that require interpretation, data work, and individualised reason- ing reduce the likelihood of plagiarism—not by restricting AI, but by making superficial or copy-paste use of AI to be unhelpful in completing the task. In parallel, students appear open to clearer citation rules and policy frameworks that treat AI not as a threat, but as a tool to be integrated transparently and ethically. As recent policy reviews note, student behav- iour improves when they are given structured, institution-wide guidance that distinguishes appropriate from inappropriate AI use (Freeman, 2025; Watkins, 2024). 1 3 Beyond Detection: How Students Use—and Hide—AI in Online… Page 19 of 23 14 In short, student behaviour around AI use in assessment is not irrational, unethical, or eva- sive. It is strategic, shaped by signals, incentives, and a rapidly changing technological land- scape. The challenge for universities is to align their expectations, policies, and assessment formats with this reality. As Coates et al. (2025) emphasise, such alignment is fundamentally a question of academic governance: boards and senates must adopt integrity metrics, resource staff training, and benchmark progress to turn policy rhetoric into everyday practice. It is important to acknowledge, however, several limitations of this study. The sample was small (n = 31, representing about 18% of the cohort) and drawn from a single UK eco- nomics programme with potential self-selection bias. These characteristics mean the find- ings are exploratory and not generalisable beyond this setting. Demographically, female and international students were somewhat over-represented among respondents compared with the cohort as a whole, which may also have shaped the patterns we observe. The reliance on self-reported data also introduces the risk of social desirability bias—that is, students may underreport AI use or overstate ethical caution to present themselves more favour- ably, despite the survey’s anonymity. While the exploratory regression offered suggestive insights, the small sample size limits the strength of any statistical claims. Finally, these findings reflect perceptions at a single point in time, before the release of more advanced AI tools and detection systems. Future research with larger, more diverse cohorts and longitu- dinal designs will be essential to build on these preliminary insights. Conclusion This paper reports on a small-scale survey of undergraduate economics students, explor- ing their perceptions, behaviours, and ethical concerns around the use of AI tools in online assessments. As AI tools become increasingly accessible, universities face urgent ques- tions–not just about detection and enforcement, but about transparency, pedagogy, and trust. This study highlights three key findings. First, while reported AI use was moderate, dis- closure was rare, driven more by fear of penalties than intent to deceive. Second, students used AI mainly for supportive tasks like rewording or idea generation, and many called for clearer citation rules to distinguish acceptable from unacceptable use. Third, students valued assessments that emphasised real-world data and interpretation–tasks where shallow AI shortcuts fall short. These findings suggest that the future of academic integrity lies not in surveillance, but in structure. Universities should prioritise assessment formats that reward authentic engagement and provide clear, actionable AI guidance. Students are not seeking to bypass learning–they are asking for clarity on how to learn ethically with new tools. Meeting that challenge requires institutions to lead with transparency, creativity, and agility. JSON: Name: authentic_assessment_ai_disclosure Title: Randomized controlled evaluation of authentic data-based assessment designs and explicit AI-disclosure policies to reduce undisclosed generative-AI use in online undergraduate assessments Short Hypothesis: Assigning students to authentic, real-world data assessments combined with explicit AI citation requirements causes a higher rate of voluntary AI-use disclosure and a lower rate of undisclosed AI-generated full-answer submissions than standard assessment formats without explicit citation rules. Related Work: Existing approaches to managing generative-AI in higher education cluster into three broad strategies: detection-and-deterrence using forensic or classifier tools; policy-based prohibition or high-penalty regimes; and pedagogical redesign aimed at authentic, applied tasks. Survey studies document widespread light-touch use of AI for editing and brainstorming, low voluntary disclosure, and high penalty anxiety, but rely predominantly on self-report and cross-sectional designs. Forensic detectors show limited reliability and high false-positive/negative rates; policy bans produce ambiguity and strategic non-disclosure; and prior proposals for authentic assessments are largely conceptual or descriptive with scarce causal evidence. Limitations across current methods include reliance on single-pass questionnaires, lack of experimental randomization, weak ground truth for AI-origin detection, inadequate cross-cultural analysis (e.g., international vs domestic students), and little systematic measurement of downstream learning outcomes when AI is integrated versus prohibited. Abstract: Problem: Universities need evidence about whether assessment design and explicit AI-use policies change student disclosure behavior and reduce undisclosed misuse of generative AI in online assessments. Approach: Conduct a randomized controlled field experiment across multiple undergraduate courses comparing (A) standard assessments with no explicit AI rules, (B) standard assessments with explicit AI citation requirements and guidance, (C) authentic, real-world data assessments with no explicit AI rules, and (D) authentic, real-world data assessments with explicit AI citation requirements. Main contribution: Provide causal estimates of the effect of assessment authenticity and citation policy on (i) voluntary disclosure rates, (ii) incidence of undisclosed AI-generated full answers (measured via combined manual review, instrumented artifacts, and detector ensembles), and (iii) student learning outcomes and perceptions. Expected outcome: Quantitative evidence of whether and how authentic task design and transparent citation rules increase disclosure and reduce undisclosed AI misuse while preserving or improving assessed learning outcomes. Experiments: Population and sampling: Recruit multiple sections across at least three distinct undergraduate courses from two universities (target total N >= 800 students). Randomization: Cluster-randomize at the tutorial/lab section level into four arms: Control (standard assessment, no AI guidance), Citation-only (standard assessment + explicit AI citation policy + citation template), Data-only (authentic data-based assessment, no AI guidance), Data+Citation (authentic data-based assessment + explicit AI citation policy + citation template). Assignment ratio 1:1:1:1. Interventions: Standard assessment = typical closed-response or essay tasks; authentic data-based = tasks requiring bespoke, time-stamped datasets and interpretation, plus submission of analysis code and short reflective write-up. Citation policy = explicit instruction specifying allowed AI uses, how to cite outputs (template), and that citation is not punitive. Measurement modalities: 1) Self-report survey immediately post-assessment: binary AI-use disclosure and Likert items on ethical anxiety; 2) Artifact collection: full submissions including code, timestamps, version history where available; 3) Detector ensemble outputs: run multiple AI-content detectors and flag high-confidence AI outputs; 4) Manual blind adjudication: independent raters evaluate flagged submissions for AI-origin or substantial AI-authorship using rubric; 5) Learning outcomes: rubric-based grading, exam performance in subsequent summative assessments; 6) Access/fairness metrics: student-reported access to paid AI tools and demographic covariates. Baselines: Status-quo (Control) and prior detection-only regime (post-hoc detector applied without design change). Evaluation metrics: Primary outcomes = disclosure rate (proportion disclosing AI use), undisclosed AI-generation rate (proportion of students with adjudicated AI-generated full answers who did not disclose), and change in learning outcomes (mean rubric score). Secondary outcomes = detector precision/recall against adjudicator labels, changes in ethical-anxiety scores, and heterogeneity by home status (domestic vs international) and language proficiency. Statistical analysis: Intention-to-treat estimation using logistic regression for binary outcomes and OLS for continuous grades, including cluster-robust standard errors at section level; pre-specified covariates: course, prior GPA, language status, and access to paid AI. Power calculation: detect a 10 percentage-point absolute increase in disclosure rate with 80% power at alpha=0.05 requires ~200 students per arm (adjust for clustering ICC=0.02). Ablations and comparisons: 1) Compare Data-only vs Control to isolate effect of task authenticity; 2) Compare Citation-only vs Control to isolate effect of explicit policy; 3) Compare Data+Citation vs Data-only and Citation-only to test interaction; 4) Detector ablation: ensemble vs single-detector performance; 5) Measurement ablation: adjudicator-only labels vs detector-only labels for robustness. Pre-registration: publicly pre-register randomization, primary outcomes, statistical models, and thresholds for detector ensemble alerts. Data handling: anonymize submissions, store audit logs, and obtain informed consent per ethics approvals. Risk Factors and Limitations: Underreporting and social desirability: voluntary self-reports may remain biased downward even under explicit citation policies. Detection reliability: AI-detection tools have limited precision and recall; manual adjudication is resource-intensive and may have inter-rater variability. Hawthorne and instruction effects: randomization and awareness may change behavior independent of intervention. Spillover and contamination: students may share materials across sections or obtain guidance from peers in other arms. External validity: results from economics and data-focused tasks may not generalize to humanities or creative-writing assessments. Cultural and equity concerns: international or non-native-English students may respond differently, limiting generalization; interventions may differentially burden students with less access to paid AI tools. Scalability and operational cost: bespoke dataset creation and manual adjudication impose instructor time and institutional cost. Ethical and privacy constraints: collecting submission artifacts, code, and AI interaction logs raises consent and data-protection requirements that may reduce participation or available data. Gaming: students may learn to evade detection or manipulate citation statements. Statistical power: cluster randomization and low baseline disclosure rates may require larger samples than available, reducing ability to detect modest effects.
